references.text: Jericho and everything in the city shall be devoted to destruction for the Lord (חֵרֶם). This shows how חֵרֶם was practiced during the conquest of Canaan, where the entire city was dedicated to destruction.
Achan took some of the devoted things (חֵרֶם), which brought God's wrath upon Israel. This illustrates the seriousness of breaking the ban on taking devoted items.
Whoever is caught with what has been devoted shall be burned with fire. The penalty is death, as Leviticus 27:29 prescribes for anything under the ban.
Israel made a vow to devote (חֵרֶם) the cities of the Canaanites if the Lord gave them victory. This shows voluntary dedication to destruction.
You shall not bring anything devoted into your house, or you will be devoted yourself. This emphasizes that חֵרֶם cannot be redeemed.
A city that has turned to idolatry must be completely devoted (חֵרֶם). Everything in it shall be burned, and none of the devoted things shall remain in your hand.
Saul was commanded to devote (חֵרֶם) the Amalekites completely—both people and animals. This shows that חֵרֶם includes a death sentence with no possibility of redemption.
The people took some of the devoted things (חֵרֶם) to offer to the Lord. Samuel rejected this, showing that devoted items cannot be repurposed.
Ahab set free a man who was meant for destruction (חֵרֶם), and the prophet declared that Ahab's life would be given in his place. This illustrates that חֵרֶם requires death.
Whoever does not appear within three days shall have all their property devoted (יָחֳרַם) and be expelled from the assembly. This shows the use of חֵרֶם in post-exilic times.
